column2: This course teaches Dr. Bardia Khosravani’s FIS method: buy shares of companies that make real profit and pay a good part of it to shareholders in cash.
The “In Dr. Khosravani’s words” boxes are his own sentences, with sources. The rest is this app’s explanation.
He didn’t make or approve this app. His full courses are at roseoj.com.
It’s like studying from a professor’s book: the book is his, but someone else wrote these notes.
FIS means working out which company really makes money and whether its price is fair. You get the information from Codal, the official site for company reports.
FLM means managing yourself: fear, greed, and how much of your money goes where.
FIS isn’t predicting charts or buying and selling every day.
Buying a share is like becoming a partner in a bakery. FIS asks how much profit the bakery makes; FLM makes sure you don’t sell your share cheap out of fear after one slow day.
This app is only teaching; it doesn’t tell you what to buy.
No method guarantees a profit. The goal is to make fewer big mistakes.
Company names in the examples are made up. “(please check)” means check that detail yourself.
A driving course doesn’t guarantee you’ll never crash, but it makes it much less likely.
First you get yourself ready: goals and personal rules.
Then market basics, then reading Codal, then the FIS method for judging profit and price.
You practise controlling your emotions (FLM) at the same time.
At the end you practise for a few months with pretend money, and then move on to harder topics.
Like learning to cook: first the tools, then the recipes, then cooking a few times for family, and finally the big party.
Choose 8 to 10 companies from several different industries, such as cement, pharma, banks and food.
Make an Excel file for each company: sales each month, profit each quarter, important events, and your own decisions.
Like the logbook you keep for your car: when it was serviced, what it cost, what broke.
Each week spend half an hour on the new Codal reports and write down the numbers.
Look at the company’s numbers first, then the share price, so the price doesn’t sway your judgement.
Before each report comes out, write down your own guess, then compare.
Practise with pretend money for at least 3 months.
Like buying a home: first you look at the size and the state of the building, then the price; otherwise a cheap price blinds you.
tsetmc: today’s share price and the number of shares.
seo.ir: the exchange rules.
ime.co.ir: prices of goods that companies sell on the commodity exchange.
The central bank and the statistics centre for inflation; Akhza for the risk-free return.
Codal is like the company’s report card; these sites are like the market price list and the city news you need next to the report card.
Split your money by when you’ll need it.
1 to 3 months of spending: a bank account. Rainy-day money (6 to 12 months of spending): somewhere safe that turns into cash quickly, such as a fixed-income fund.
1 to 3-year goals: low-swing places such as Akhza, fixed income or gold.
Only money you won’t need for at least 5 years goes into stocks.
You don’t buy shares with next month’s rent money; because if the market falls, you’d have to sell cheap to pay the rent.
Write one page of rules for yourself and sign it.
What return you want and how big a fall you can live with.
The most of your money that can be in one stock or one industry, and when you’ll review.
Things you’ll never do: borrow for stocks, buy on channel signals.
Like a shopping list before going to the market: it helps you not buy things you don’t need in a moment of excitement.
Save at the start of the month, not from whatever is left at the end.
In Dr. Khosravani’s view, keeping money somewhere that earns less than inflation is really a loss; that’s only a place to park money briefly.
Keep part of your assets in gold or silver to protect the value of your money.
Having cash isn’t a reason to buy; buy when something is cheaper than it’s worth. And the best investment: learning.
If bread gets 40% more expensive each year and your money earns 25% a year, at the end of the year you can buy less bread.
